slides.text:
Two sessions on the corners of slices:

- **Session 1:** the `nil` slice against the empty one, and `clear`
- **Session 2:** cutting again and again, and the traps of comparing slices

A nil slice is a slice with no values behind it. An empty slice has a window of size zero. For most code they act the same: their length is 0 and a loop over them does nothing.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
nil list    -> no window at all
empty list  -> a window with 0 boxes
both have length 0

slides.text: They differ only when compared with `nil`. So to ask whether a slice has values, test its length, not nil. And `clear` sets every value of a slice back to its zero value, without changing the length.

exercises.title: Nil or empty
exercises.guide: Three ways to get a slice with no values.

chunks.guide: A declared slice, an empty literal and a made one.
All three have length 0, but only the first is nil. They print the same.
chunks.text:
fmt.Println(len(a), len(b), len(c))
    fmt.Println(a == nil, b == nil, c == nil)
    fmt.Println(a, b, c)

exercises.title: Nothing to walk
exercises.guide: Loop over a nil slice and see nothing happen.

chunks.guide: Ranging over a nil slice is fine: it does zero turns.
Its length is 0, and cutting it gives a slice with no values.

exercises.title: Is it empty
exercises.guide: Print whether the slice has no values, then whether it is nil.

exercises.title: Clear values
exercises.guide: Set the values of a slice to zero.

chunks.guide: `clear` sets every value of a slice to its zero value. Cleared through a piece, the original changes too.

notes.text: Zeroes the values, and the length stays.

chunks.text:
scores := []int{1, 2, 3, 4}
    part := scores[:2]
    clear(part)
    fmt.Println(scores, len(scores))

chunks.guide: Clearing the whole slice zeroes every value.

exercises.title: What does it print?
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `part` holds indexes 1 and 2 of `scores`. `clear` zeroes those two values and removes nothing, so `part` keeps length 2 and `scores` shows the zeros.

slides.text:
A cut can be assigned back to the same variable. `s = s[1:]` drops the first value and `s = s[:len(s)-1]` drops the last. Nothing is copied: the slice just looks at fewer values.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
list looks at boxes 1, 2, 3, 4
list = list from 1
list looks at boxes 2, 3, 4

slides.text: A cut of a cut counts its indexes from where the first one starts, but it still shares the original values. And two slices cannot be compared with `==`: only a comparison with `nil` is allowed. Comparing values takes a loop.

exercises.title: Drop the ends
exercises.guide: Shrink a slice from both sides.

chunks.guide: Cut from index 1 and keep the result in the same variable.
Cut up to the last index to drop the last value.

exercises.title: Take from the front
exercises.guide: Take values one by one from the front of a slice.

chunks.guide: Read the first value, then drop it from the slice.
chunks.text:
queue := []string{"a", "b", "c"}
    next := queue[0]
    queue = queue[1:]
    fmt.Println(next, queue)

chunks.guide: Do it again for the next value.
chunks.text:
next = queue[0]
    queue = queue[1:]
    fmt.Println(next, queue, len(queue))

exercises.title: Take the next job
exercises.guide: Take the first job and drop it from the slice.

exercises.title: Cut a cut
exercises.guide: Cut a piece out of a piece.

chunks.guide: A piece of a piece. Its indexes count from where it starts.
All three look at the same values.
`==` does not work between two slices. Different lengths are never equal.
Then compare the values position by position.
Same values in the same order are equal.

exercises.title: A piece of a piece
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `mid` is scores[1:3] and `tail` is mid[1:], which is scores[2:3]. So `tail[0]` is `scores[2]`. The value shows in all three, and `tail` holds one value.

exercises.title: Why does it not compile?
exercises.guide: Read the message, then pick the cause.
exercises.code:
./main.go:9:14: invalid operation: a == b
(slice can only be compared to nil)
options: `==` only works on numbers and strings
Both slices must be declared with `make`
Slices can only be compared with nil
exercises.explanation: Slices have no `==` between them: the only comparison allowed is with `nil`. To compare values, loop over them.
